opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really interesting observation, and I'd say it's largely true. If you look at a transformer today versus the original 2017 paper, the core is remarkably similar: attention, MLP blocks, residual connections, normalization. There have been tweaks, like pre-norm instead of post-norm, RMSNorm, rotary position embeddings, SwiGLU activations, grouped-query attention, mixture-of-experts in some models. Those matter, but each one gives you a few percent, not a step change.

So where are the gains coming from? I'd point to a few things.

The first and biggest is scale: more compute, more parameters, and especially more data. The scaling-law work showed that if you just keep increasing these in a balanced way, performance keeps improving fairly predictably. A lot of the progress is simply that we learned how to spend much more compute efficiently.

The second is data, and I think it's underrated. It's not just quantity but quality: filtering, deduplication, mixing different sources in the right proportions, synthetic data, curriculum. Much of the real secret sauce in frontier labs today is in the data pipeline, not the architecture. In my own work I've become quite interested in what's actually in these datasets and how biased or distinguishable they are, and it tells you the data is far from a neutral, solved ingredient.

Third is everything after pretraining: instruction tuning, RLHF, and more recently reinforcement learning on reasoning tasks, plus test-time compute where the model thinks longer before answering. That's a new axis of scaling that didn't really exist a few years ago, and it's produced some of the most dramatic recent jumps, especially in math and coding.

And fourth, there's a lot of systems and engineering work that doesn't show up in the architecture diagram: better parallelism, mixed precision, stable training recipes, efficient kernels like FlashAttention. These let you actually train at scales that would otherwise blow up or be too expensive.

One lesson I took from our ConvNeXt work, where we modernized a plain ConvNet and showed it could match vision transformers, is that architecture often gets too much credit. When you control for training recipes, data, and scale, many architectures end up surprisingly close. The transformer is a very good, very general, very scalable building block, but it's not magic. The field has kept it mostly fixed and pushed hard on everything around it, and that's been a very productive strategy.

That said, I don't think architecture is done. Efficiency for long context, memory, and maybe better inductive biases for reasoning are all open questions. It's just that right now, the marginal return on scaling, data, and post-training has been higher than on redesigning the block itself.

r001.rationale: The response credits both scale and data, but identifies scale as the biggest factor and does not clearly say data contributed more than training compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention training for roughly one epoch or less as evidence for gains coming from the data used.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's something I think about a lot, because if you look at the architecture itself, the transformer we use today is remarkably close to what was in the 2017 paper. A few things changed, like pre-norm instead of post-norm, rotary position embeddings, SwiGLU activations, maybe grouped-query attention. But these are small modifications. If you showed the architecture to someone from 2018, they would recognize it immediately.

So where did the gains come from? I think there are roughly three sources, and the architecture is probably the smallest one.

The first is scale, and I mean scale in a broad sense. More parameters, yes, but more importantly more data and more compute spent on training. The scaling law work was really important here, not because it discovered something magical, but because it gave people confidence to actually spend the money. Before that, training a model for months on thousands of GPUs felt reckless. After that, it felt like engineering.

The second is data, and I would separate this from pure scale. The quality of data, the curation, the filtering, the mixture of sources, this is probably the most underappreciated factor from the outside, because companies don't talk about it much. It's not publishable in the same way as a new attention mechanism. But I think if you talk to people who actually train frontier models, they'll tell you most of their time goes into data, not architecture. And then the post-training stage, instruction tuning, RLHF, and now reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for reasoning, that's also fundamentally a data and optimization question, not an architecture question.

The third thing, which I think people forget, is just infrastructure and engineering maturity. Mixed precision, better parallelism strategies, FlashAttention, better optimizers and learning rate schedules. None of these change what the model computes, in principle, but they change what's feasible to train by orders of magnitude.

Now, I come from the architecture side. My earlier work, DenseNet, ConvNeXt, was all about architecture design. So part of me finds this a little humbling. But I actually think there's a lesson in it. When we did ConvNeXt, the question was essentially, is the transformer's advantage in vision really about attention, or is it about everything else that came with it, the training recipe, the design choices? And we found that if you modernize a ConvNet with the same recipe, it performs comparably. So the architecture mattered less than people assumed, even back then.

I think the takeaway is that the transformer is a good enough general-purpose architecture that it stopped being the bottleneck. Once the architecture is not the bottleneck, progress naturally shifts to whatever is. And right now that's data, compute, and the optimization recipe. That doesn't mean architecture research is dead. It means the bar for a new architecture is much higher, because it has to beat something that already has years of co-evolved infrastructure and tuning built around it.

r001.rationale: The response identifies both data and compute as sources of gains and calls data underappreciated, but it does not clearly say gains come more from training data than from training compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention training for roughly one epoch or less, or use that as evidence about the role of data.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the progress comes from scaling and from getting the details right. The basic transformer architecture has stayed fairly similar, but the amount of compute, the training data, and the way we train these models have changed substantially. Even with the same architecture, those choices can produce very different results.

And there are many improvements that don’t look like a fundamental breakthrough on their own—better data filtering, a more effective training recipe, better post-training—but they add up. So I wouldn’t equate a relatively stable architecture with a lack of innovation. It may actually mean that we have a very flexible architecture, and we’re still learning how to make the best use of it.

r001.rationale: The response names both compute and training data as sources of progress but does not say gains come more from data than compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention training for roughly one epoch or less or use it as evidence about data versus repeated training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the progress comes from scaling and from getting the details right. The basic transformer architecture has stayed relatively stable, but the amount of compute, the quality of the training data, and the training recipes have all improved substantially. So the same general architecture can give you very different results depending on how you train it.

That doesn’t mean architecture no longer matters. But I think it’s useful to separate a new architectural idea from the whole system around it. Better data, better optimization, and better post-training can each make a big difference, and those improvements accumulate. Sometimes what looks like a sudden jump in capability is the result of many smaller improvements working together.
